notes.title: Chapter map: Listening

headings.text: 🔬 To explore: is AssemblyAI (or Cartesia) better than Deepgram for us?
🏷️ Landscape (as of Oct 2026, LiveKit Inference STT)

notes.html:
How sound becomes words: a shared "is someone speaking?" signal, a streaming recogniser that keeps pace with speech, and the vocabulary, language and measurement choices that decide whether the words that matter come out right.

Where this sits

capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe

Reading order

# Note Tier Stage You'll understand
1 Voice activity detection CORE detect the shared speech signal, its two events, and what it doesn't do
2 Streaming speech-to-text CORE transcribe interim vs final, the settings that matter, warm connections
3 Vocabulary and keyterms SUPPORTING transcribe biasing toward domain words, and what it buys
4 Accent, language, code-switching SUPPORTING transcribe en-IN vs multi, and fairness across accents
5 Measuring recognition SUPPORTING observe term recall over WER, goldens, gates
– Diarization BREADTH transcribe a second-voice signal, never a verdict

Owners

Concept Home
Speech start and stop events, Silero settings VAD
Interim and final transcripts, STT settings, warm sockets streaming STT
Keyterm prompting, the term budget vocabulary
Locale vs multilingual, per-cohort accuracy accent and language
WER, term recall, goldens, gates measuring recognition
End of turn (the decision VAD's "stop" feeds) endpointing
Noise suppression and echo before VAD Audio cleanup

Decide: which STT setup?

Ask in order If yes → Because
1. Must domain terms be right (technical, medical, legal)? locale model + keyterms; gate on term recall the terms carry the meaning
2. Do people mix languages mid-sentence? test multi or a code-switching model on your goldens first it may cost term accuracy
3. Is the model batch-only (e.g. Whisper)? StreamAdapter + VAD buffers until speech ends: no interims
4. Do you need the STT to end turns? turn_detection="stt" with a vendor that endpoints well otherwise keep vendor endpointing off

🔊 Our system in one table

Stage What we run Status Measured
detect Silero, prewarmed per process ~1 ms per ~30 ms frame
transcribe Deepgram Nova-3 en-IN, interims, punctuate, smart format, diarization, ≤ 100 keyterms, endpointing off STT delay p50 404 ms
transcribe keyterms in priority order: plan → topics → section → stack → base recall 96%, WER 11.2% (synthetic Indian-accent voice)
transcribe en-IN over multi term recall 86% vs 76%
observe goldens with gates on claimed categories gated: recall 99%, WER 1.7%

To explore: is AssemblyAI (or Cartesia) better than Deepgram for us?

Short answer, as of 16 Oct 2026: unknown for our audio. Every head-to-head number found is published by one of the two vendors, each wins its own benchmark, and no independent streaming comparison of current models turned up (search, 16 Oct 2026).

Deepgram (what we run) AssemblyAI
Models on LiveKit Inference (16 Oct 2026) Flux, Nova-3, Nova-2 Universal-3.6 Pro, Universal-3.5 Pro, Universal-Streaming (English), Universal-Streaming Multilingual
Vocabulary keyterm (Nova-3) keyterms_prompt, all streaming models
End of turn Flux has its own; Nova-3 endpointing (we turn it off) Universal-3.6 Pro: punctuation-based (turn_detection="stt"); Universal-Streaming: phrase endpointing model
Code-switching nova-3:multi (cost us 10 points of term recall) Universal-3.6/3.5 Pro and Multilingual: automatic language detection and code-switching
Extras diarization, smart format diarization, Medical Mode, Voice Focus noise suppression
Vendor's own claims lower latency and WER on Deepgram's test set 307 ms vs 516 ms median latency at Universal-Streaming's June 2025 launch; fewer missed emails and phone numbers

Cartesia STT, a third option (LiveKit, 16 Oct 2026): cartesia/ink-2 is English-only, has no word-aligned transcripts (so no adaptive interruption with it) and can end turns with turn_detection="stt"; cartesia/ink-whisper covers many languages and is picked automatically for non-English. LiveKit's page states no keyterm support and no accuracy or latency figure. Cartesia is better known for its TTS (see Speaking: to explore).

Why it's worth testing: AssemblyAI's code-switching models might handle Hinglish without the term-recall loss multi cost us, and that is our known weak point.

How to test (one change per run, same harness):

  1. Add AssemblyAI (and Cartesia Ink if keyterms aren't needed for the test) as STT options behind the same interface (LiveKit Inference or the livekit-agents[assemblyai] plugin).
  2. Run goldens/stt_tts with the same keyterm list on both: term recall and WER per category, especially code_switch, tech_vocab, numbers.
  3. Measure transcription_delay and late-final rate from India on live calls.
  4. Compare cost per audio minute at our volume.
  5. Decide on term recall first, Hinglish second, latency third.

Sources: LiveKit — Cartesia STT · AssemblyAI — AssemblyAI vs Deepgram for voice agents (vendor) · DEV Community comparison · Smallest.ai — most accurate real-time transcription APIs in 2026 (vendor) · LiveKit — AssemblyAI STT.

Open Indic models: IISc's SraVaani-0.5-live (streaming, 63 Indian languages) is a fourth option for the code-switch case, self-hosted; see Indic speech at IISc.

Landscape (as of Oct 2026, LiveKit Inference STT)

Vendor Models listed by LiveKit
Deepgram Flux, Nova-3, Nova-2
AssemblyAI Universal-3.6 Pro, Universal-3.5 Pro, Universal-Streaming
Cartesia Ink 2, Ink Whisper
Google gemini-3.5-transcribe-live
OpenAI gpt-live-transcribe
Speechmatics linden-1 (Enhanced and Standard retired 5 Oct 2026)
Others Inworld inworld-stt-1; xAI stt-1, stt-2

Game Day

Q8 partial vs final · Q17 STT degrades · Q20 misheard number · Q36 technical vocabulary · Q37 en-IN not multilingual · Q49 measure voice quality

notes.title: Voice Activity Detection — Is Someone Speaking Right Now?
notes.html:
References

LiveKit — Silero VAD plugin (read 16 Oct 2026) · Silero VAD · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/transcript_quality.md §3 · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/interview_prep/03-vad-turn-detection.md

TL;DR

VAD is a tiny model that scores each ~30 ms audio frame for "is this speech?". It knows sound from silence and nothing else: it doesn't clean audio, doesn't know words, and doesn't know whether a turn is over. Everything that reacts to speech (barge-in, the endpoint clock, telling the STT to finalise) starts from its two events: speech started and speech stopped.

Stage: capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe · per frame

Flow: frameP(speech) ─above threshold for min_speechSTART ─below threshold for min_silenceENDendpoint clock + STT finalise

Recall

Prompt Answer
What VAD outputs per frame a speech probability
Its two events start of speech, end of speech
Three things it does not do clean audio, transcribe, decide the turn is over
Who listens to "speech started" while the agent talks? barge-in
Who listens to "speech stopped"? the endpoint clock and the STT (finalise now)
Silero sample rates in LiveKit 8 kHz and 16 kHz only
Draw P(speech) over 3 s with a pause, a cough and a word threshold line; start and end events with their minimum durations

The idea

Without it: every component listens to raw audio and guesses separately; the STT runs on silence, barge-in fires on hum, and nothing agrees on when speech ended.

It does: gives the whole pipeline one cheap, fast, shared answer to "is there speech?", on CPU, per frame.

It costs: a threshold. Too low and noise becomes speech (false barge-ins); too high and soft speakers are missed. Clean audio upstream makes the threshold easier.

How it works

Event Who acts on it
speech started, agent speaking barge-in stops the agent
speech started silence watch disarmed; interim STT begins
speech stopped endpoint clock starts; STT is told to finalise
speech stopped, ≥ 0.25 s turn detector may be asked

At 16 kHz, Silero's 512-sample window is 32 ms (computed); the model is under 2 MB and runs on CPU.

Knobs

Knob Default (LiveKit Silero, Oct 2026) Raise it → Lower it →
activation_threshold 0.5 ignores noise; may miss soft speech catches soft speech; noise becomes speech
min_speech_duration 0.05 s ignores clicks reacts sooner
min_silence_duration 0.55 s fewer split utterances, later end event earlier end; must stay ≥ 0.25 s with the turn detector
prefix_padding_duration 0.5 s keeps the first syllable less buffered audio
sample_rate 16 000 – 8 000 for phone audio
Prewarm load per job – load once per process (setup_fnc → proc.userdata["vad"])

🔊 In our system

What Value Status Why / source
VAD Silero, prewarmed per process so the first turn doesn't pay for loading as_built §2 row 4
Cost ~1 ms per ~30 ms frame, under 2 MB interview_prep/03, transcript_quality §3
Upstream cleaning browser AEC + NS + AGC, then Krisp nc in the agent as_built rows 1, 3
Drives barge-in (vad mode, 0.4 s), STT finalise (vendor endpointing off) meghdootam/main.py

Measure it

  • Metric — false-start rate on noise-only recordings, missed-start rate on soft speech, and false-interruption rate in calls.
  • See it — START_OF_SPEECH / END_OF_SPEECH events against a recording; plot P(speech) for a noisy call.
  • Bounded by — barge-in's resume after a false interruption; minimum speech duration.

Pitfalls

Using VAD silence as end of turn

  • Why it's tempting: "speech stopped" sounds like "turn over".
  • Why it's wrong: thinking pauses are silent too; VAD alone cuts off every thinker.
  • Think instead: VAD starts the clock; the turn detector and the endpoint window decide.

Tuning the threshold to fix a noisy room

  • Why it's tempting: it's the one number that reacts to noise.
  • Why it's wrong: raising it to ignore a fan also ignores quiet speakers.
  • Think instead: clean the audio first (AEC, noise suppression), then keep the default threshold.

Connections

… → clean → detect → transcribe → … — the shared "speech?" signal.

  • triggers barge-in and starts the endpoint clock.
  • tells the STT when to finalise.
  • works better after echo cancellation and noise suppression.
  • Say it: Q6

notes.title: Streaming Speech-to-Text — Interim and Final Words, While They Speak
notes.html:
References

LiveKit — STT models (read 16 Oct 2026) · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/interview_prep/01-stt.md · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/voice_pipeline_design.md §5.1 · ~/Projects/convo_agentic/meghdootam/main.py (deepgram.STT)

TL;DR

A streaming recogniser listens over one open connection and emits interim guesses every few hundred milliseconds, revising them as more audio arrives, then a final transcript per phrase. Interims let work start during speech; finals are what you commit. The STT's own endpointing is a separate feature, and usually switched off.

Stage: capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe · per turn

Flow: audio framesinterim "we used Kaf"interim "we used Kafka for"final "We used Kafka for ordering."commit when the turn ends

Recall

Prompt Answer
Interim vs final a revisable guess while speaking vs the settled text for a phrase
What interims are used for early work: preemptive generation, the guard, background analysis
Why the stream must open before first speech a cold connect (TLS + WebSocket) costs hundreds of ms on the first turn
What a non-streaming model needs in LiveKit StreamAdapter + VAD: buffer until speech ends, then transcribe
Formatting that changes meaning punctuation and smart formatting ("300K QPS" vs "three hundred K")
Draw interim and final events under a 4 s utterance interims every ~300 ms, a final at each phrase end, commit after the endpoint wait

The idea

Without it: record the whole turn, upload, transcribe: seconds after the person stops, and nothing can start early.

It does: turns recognition into a stream that keeps pace with speech, so the transcript is almost complete the moment the person stops.

It costs: interims are wrong and get rewritten, so anything built on them must tolerate revision; and the last final phrase can still arrive after the endpoint window closes.

How it works

Setting Why it matters
Interim results on the input for every "start early" mechanism
Vendor endpointing off one end-of-turn authority (endpointing)
Punctuation on feeds the turn detector and readable transcripts
Smart formatting on numbers and units in the form the scorer reads
Language fixed or multi accent and language
Vocabulary keyterm prompting

Under the hood (interview_prep/01): log-mel features → a transformer or conformer encoder → streaming decoders (CTC, RNN-T) that attend to past audio and a little future, which is what makes interims possible.

Knobs

Knob Default Raise it → Lower it →
Interim results provider-specific early work possible –
Vendor endpointing on in most plugins – off: the turn detector decides
Language per model; Deepgram multi for mixed speech (LiveKit, Oct 2026) multi: captures code-switching, mixed scripts fixed locale: higher accuracy on that language
Connection per plugin; pooled warm before first speech cold first turn

🔊 In our system

What Value Status Why / source
Model Deepgram Nova-3, en-IN, via the LiveKit plugin main.py
Settings interims on (~300 ms), punctuate, smart format, diarization, keyterms, endpointing_ms=0 design §5.1; the plugin sends Finalize when VAD ends speech
STT delay p50 404 ms as_built §3, 30 days to 16 Oct 2026
Late finals 23% of turns waited past the window for the final words (median 3 words) FLOW §1, 71 turns; cause not established
Confidence used only to ask for a repeat; never reaches the scorer design §5.4 (fairness)
Backup STT none yet; a second vendor behind the same interface as_built row 5

Measure it

  • Metric — transcription_delay per turn, interim cadence, and late-final rate; accuracy in measuring recognition.
  • See it — INTERIM_TRANSCRIPT and FINAL_TRANSCRIPT events with timestamps against VAD's end-of-speech.
  • Bounded by — a repeat request on low confidence; the turn commits when the final arrives.

Pitfalls

Building on interims as if they were final

  • Why it's tempting: they arrive early and look right most of the time.
  • Why it's wrong: they are rewritten; a decision on "we used Kaf…" can be undone by the final.
  • Think instead: start work on interims or finals, but key it by turn and redo it on the committed text.

Opening the STT stream on first speech

  • Why it's tempting: no idle connection to pay for.
  • Why it's wrong: the first turn pays the cold connect, which is the turn the person judges the product on.
  • Think instead: open and warm the stream at session start.

Connections

… → detect → transcribe → endpoint → … — turns sound into the words every later stage reads.

  • finalised by VAD; committed by endpointing.
  • feeds early preemptive generation.
  • improved by keyterms.
  • Say it: Q8 · Q17

notes.title: Vocabulary — Keyterm Prompting and What It Buys
notes.html:
References

LiveKit — Keyterm management (read 16 Oct 2026) · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/voice_quality_goldens.md §4 · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/transcript_quality.md §4 · ~/Projects/convo_agentic/meghdootam/voice/vocab.py, topic_terms.py

TL;DR

A recogniser picks the most likely words, and "item potent" is more common than "idempotent". Keyterm prompting hands the model a short list of the words this conversation is likely to contain, so ambiguous audio resolves toward them. It breaks ties; it can't invent a word that wasn't said or rescue unclear audio.

Stage: capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe · per session

Flow: plan + topics + stack≤ 100 terms in priority ordersent with the sessionambiguous audio decoded toward them

Recall

Prompt Answer
What keyterm prompting does biases decoding toward listed terms when the audio is ambiguous
What it can't do create unsaid words or fix very unclear audio
Nova-3 vs Nova-2 plain terms (keyterm) vs (term, boost) weights (keywords)
Why order the list a cap cuts from the end
Can terms change mid-session in LiveKit? yes, update_options (Oct 2026)
Draw the term list as a priority stack plan terms on top, base list at the bottom, the cap line

The idea

Without it: the terms the conversation turns on are the ones the recogniser gets wrong ("BRAFQL gateway", "UAM killed"), and the person looks like they can't name their own tools.

It does: supplies context per session, from what the session is about.

It costs: a budget (Deepgram caps keyterm prompting at about 500 tokens); a bloated list dilutes the bias.

How it works

Priority Source Example
1 the plan's own terms (JD, topic, revision) functools.wraps
2 names of the topics in play Decorators
3 curated terms per section (Python, DSA, LLD, HLD, Cloud, Java, React) useEffect, p99
4 the profile's stack FastAPI, Postgres
5 base backend list (66 terms) Kafka, idempotency

LiveKit (Oct 2026) keeps one keyterm set per session and maps it to each provider: Deepgram keyterm, AssemblyAI keyterms_prompt, Speechmatics additional_vocab; providers without support log a warning. Optional automatic detection adds terms after transcript corroboration.

Knobs

Knob Default Raise it → Lower it →
List size provider cap more coverage, weaker bias per term stronger bias, more gaps
Order – plan first: what this call is about wins the cap –
Automatic detection (LiveKit) off learns terms mid-call –

🔊 In our system

What Value Status Why / source
List ≤ 100 terms per session, priority as above topic_terms.py
Effect (synthetic voices, 24 Sep 2026) term recall 79–83% → 89% (US voices); prod config en-IN + keyterms on an Indian-accent voice: 96%, WER 11.2% goldens §4
Gated categories on prod recall 99%, WER 1.7%: pass goldens §4
Not in the list 50% recall goldens §4, reported not gated
A miss HLD not boosted on a Python mock: "p99" heard as "page 99" transcript_quality §4; mocks without topics now boost HLD first

Measure it

  • Metric — key-term recall per category, with and without the list; the out-of-list category shows what the list can't fix.
  • See it — the goldens harness (python -m goldens.stt_tts.run), and misheard terms in real transcripts.
  • Bounded by — the model layer reading past slips ("item potency" still meant idempotency).

Pitfalls

Boosting everything that might come up

  • Why it's tempting: more terms seem safer.
  • Why it's wrong: the cap cuts the list, and a long list weakens each term; the important ones may be dropped.
  • Think instead: order by what this session is about and keep it short.

Treating synthetic-voice recall as real accuracy

  • Why it's tempting: the numbers are high and repeatable.
  • Why it's wrong: studio-clean synthetic speech overstates accuracy against a laptop mic.
  • Think instead: use synthetic goldens as a regression baseline; record real speakers for the truth.

Connections

… → transcribe → … — the vocabulary half of recognition quality.

  • configures streaming STT.
  • measured by measuring recognition.
  • mirrored on output by pronunciation.
  • Say it: Q36 · Q20

notes.title: Accent, Language and Code-Switching
notes.html:
References

~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/voice_pipeline_design.md §5.4 · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/decision_rationale.md §12 · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/voice_quality_goldens.md §4, §6 · LiveKit — STT models

TL;DR

Pick the recognition language for what the conversation must get right. A locale model (en-IN) is more accurate on that language's terms; a multilingual model (multi) captures code-switching but returns mixed scripts and loses accuracy. Whatever you pick, accuracy will differ by accent, so it must never leak into anything that judges the speaker.

Stage: capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe · design time

Flow: what must be right?locale model + keytermsmultimeasure per accent cohort either way

Recall

Prompt Answer
Locale vs multilingual higher accuracy on one language vs code-switching with mixed scripts
What we measured, multi vs en-IN technical-term recall 86% → 76%
What happens to Hinglish on en-IN? it comes back empty
The mitigation ask the person to repeat in English
Why STT confidence never reaches the scorer accuracy varies by accent; letting it in would score accent
Draw the decision as a two-column table locale vs multi: accuracy, scripts, code-switching, downstream effects

The idea

Without a decision: multi is left on "to be inclusive", and every downstream reader (keyterm list, prompts, quoted evidence) receives mixed Latin and Devanagari text.

It does: chooses the language for the product's job, states the cost, and builds a recovery for the speech it won't handle.

It costs: some people's speech is handled worse, by design; that has to be measured and visible, not hidden.

How it works

Locale (en-IN) Multilingual (multi)
Technical-term recall (ours, 24 Sep 2026) 86% 76%
Code-switched speech empty transcript captured
Output script Latin mixed Latin + Devanagari
Keyterm list, prompts, evidence quotes work as written disrupted
When to choose the words must be right (technical, medical, legal) the meaning must be caught across languages

LiveKit (Oct 2026): set language on the STT; Deepgram nova-3:multi for mixed speech; auto:<lang> lets LiveKit Inference pick a model per language.

Knobs

Knob Options Trade
Recognition language locale, multi, auto per language accuracy vs coverage
Repeat request on low confidence or empty transcript recovers speech, costs a turn
Per-cohort tuning endpoint windows, thresholds fairness vs one simple config

🔊 In our system

What Value Status Why / source
Language en-IN, decided 24 Sep 2026 decision_rationale §12; goldens D1
Code-switching tolerated, not supported; recall 50% in goldens goldens §4
Recovery ask to repeat in English designed, not built
Fairness confidence never leaves STT; per-cohort accuracy specified, nothing measured yet design §5.4, decision_rationale weak point 3

Measure it

  • Metric — WER and term recall per accent cohort; empty-transcript rate on code-switched speech.
  • See it — goldens split by voice; real recordings labelled by cohort.
  • Bounded by — a repeat request; confidence kept out of scoring.

Pitfalls

Turning on multi to be inclusive

  • Why it's tempting: it handles more speakers on paper.
  • Why it's wrong: for technical speech it lost 10 points of term recall, and mixed scripts break every downstream reader.
  • Think instead: choose for the words that must be right, and build the recovery for the rest.

Assuming one accuracy number covers everyone

  • Why it's tempting: the average looks good.
  • Why it's wrong: a speaker transcribed at 88% looks vaguer to a scoring model, and vagueness is a scoring signal.
  • Think instead: report accuracy per cohort and treat a gap as a release blocker.

Connections

… → transcribe → … — who the recogniser serves well.

  • configures streaming STT.
  • also shapes language-aware pause handling.
  • measured by measuring recognition.
  • open Indic models to try: SraVaani and Vaani-LID (IISc).
  • Say it: Q37 · Q50

notes.title: Diarization — Who Spoke, as a Signal
notes.html:
References

~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/voice_pipeline_design.md §5.3 · LiveKit — Speaker diarization

TL;DR

Diarization labels which speaker said each segment. In a one-person call it's useful only as a signal that a second voice is present, and it is noisy: household speech and one speaker split across labels after a pause both look like "two speakers".

Stage: capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe · per turn

The idea

Looks like a second speaker Really Rule
a voice never in dialogue with the person background speech ignore
one voice split after a long pause diarization churn ignore
a second voice interleaved within the person's turn possible coaching report as a signal for a human, never a verdict

🔊 In our system

Deepgram diarization on; Sentinel reports a second voice only when interleaved within a turn; noise suppression weakens the signal, accepted (design §5.3, fact sheet §7.4).

Connections

a setting of streaming STT; one of the three overlap jobs in backchannels and overlap.

notes.title: Measuring Recognition — WER, Term Recall, Goldens
notes.html:
References

~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/voice_quality_goldens.md §2–4 · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/transcript_quality.md §7 · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/interview_prep/01-stt.md §5

TL;DR

WER counts every wrong word equally, so it measures the recogniser, not the conversation. For a domain agent, track term recall on the words that carry meaning, gate only the categories you claim to support, and treat synthetic audio as a regression baseline, not the truth.

Stage: capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → … → observe · design time

Flow: golden sentencesaudio (recorded or synthetic)transcribe with prod configWER + term recall per categorygate

Recall

Prompt Answer
WER formula (substitutions + insertions + deletions) ÷ reference words
Why term recall beats WER here a wrong "the" costs nothing; a wrong "Kafka" changes the answer
Our gates term recall ≥ 90%, WER ≤ 15% on claimed categories
What is reported but not gated out-of-list terms, code-switching
Why synthetic audio isn't enough it's studio-clean and overstates accuracy
Draw the golden loop sentences → audio → STT → metrics per category → gate → change one parameter

The idea

Without it: "it sounded fine" on a demo, and the vocabulary failures appear only in real calls.

It does: a fixed set of sentences, the production config, a few metrics per category, and a gate, so every change to the STT config is measured.

It costs: recordings from real speakers, which are the slow, valuable part.

How it works

Metric Measures Gate (ours)
Key-term recall share of domain terms that survive ≥ 90% on claimed categories
WER all word errors ≤ 15% on claimed categories
Semantic WER errors weighted by meaning not used yet
RTF (real-time factor) processing time ÷ audio time; must be < 1 to stream –
Per-cohort WER the same, by accent group specified, not measured

Gate only what you claim. Gating code-switching (tolerated, not supported) would hide what the category is there to show.

Knobs

Knob Our value Trade
Audio source recorded if present, else three synthetic voices realism vs effort
Categories gated tech vocab, numbers (recall), Indian context, homophone traps –
Noise added brown noise + 100 Hz hum at 15, 10, 5 dB SNR tests robustness without recordings

🔊 In our system

What Value Status Why / source
Prod config, Indian-accent synthetic voice recall 96%, WER 11.2% goldens §4, 24 Sep 2026
By category tech vocab 99% · homophones 100% · Indian context 100% · numbers 95% · out-of-list 50% · code-switch 50% goldens §4
Noise at most 3–4 points of recall lost, down to 5 dB SNR: noise is not the main loss transcript_quality §7
Main losses vocabulary gaps, turn splits mid-answer, words misheard even when boosted transcript_quality §7
Next record real voices reading the 20 sentences goldens §3

Measure it

  • Metric — the gates above, per release; per-cohort numbers once recordings exist.
  • See it — python -m goldens.stt_tts.run --only stt (add --noise for the noise study).
  • Bounded by — one parameter changed per run, so a regression has one cause.

Pitfalls

Optimising WER

  • Why it's tempting: it's the standard number and easy to compute.
  • Why it's wrong: a config can lower WER on filler words while losing the terms that matter.
  • Think instead: gate on term recall for the words the product turns on.

Measuring only clean audio

  • Why it's tempting: synthetic voices are free and repeatable.
  • Why it's wrong: a laptop mic in a room is the real input; clean audio overstates accuracy.
  • Think instead: add noise and real recordings; keep synthetic as the regression line.

Connections

… → transcribe → … → observe — how recognition is judged.

  • measures keyterms and the language choice.
  • part of evaluating a voice agent.
  • Say it: Q49
